content:
I am getting very close to being able to open my repo to the community, and am unsure about whether it should be in Projects, in AI- authored projects, or somewhere else entirely.

The project is the result of six years of independent study and all of the mathematics in this respect are my own. However, in order to formalize my work in lean in a timely manner, I needed to use AI, which is responsible for the vast majority of the actual code in my project. This occurred under intense and constant moderation on my part, however, and workable code could only be produced with strong prompting either in "chat" form or in latex code from the papers I have written describing my efforts, usually a combination of the two. None the less, an AI wrote it, and there is absolutely a difference between my less-than-formal personal notation and the results in lean: An example being, I have an intuitive understanding that a given transformation I make is a bijection and say as much in my own terms, but the AI shows me how to actually prove this in lean.

I am assuming the community would prefer to have this here, but I don't know so I will ask first.

I would also strongly suggest using stickies here on Zulip: as an uninitiated (to mathlib) physicist who loves math, coming here is like getting lost in a library and the tooltips are rather limited. I only recently found out that Comparator and formalization.yamls are a thing (and I would also highly suggest some entry-level user guides -it took me three days to figure out how to get comparator to run with my libaries), and I can see there are a LOT of repeat questions in the AI section with what looks to be some degree of exhaustion from the people answering these questions. A sticky would go a long way to solving this problem on both ends, and they are almost universally recognized across forum formats. I'm not sure why we don't have them here, or if I just missed them somewhow.

I think this question is kind of fundamental. Although i'm not a mathematician, i think i know where i myself draw the line.

  • Did the AI wrote the definitions itself? If yes, then it's mainly AI authored in my view
  • Did i wrote myself the definitions, but the AI wrote the lemmas and theorems of significance ? If the answer is yes, then it's mainly AI authored in my view
  • Did i wrote myself the definitions, lemmas, theorems of importance but let the AI write the proofs and write some unimportant sub-lemmas ? i would say the result is assisted proofs by AI, mainly authored by a human.

That's where i draw the line. But others may have different opinions about this.

Yes I definitely appreciate a hearty discussion on all things AI, but my purpose here is to find out how the professionals who run this site define things, as well as give a little feedback from my own perspective being midway through the process now..

But ok i'll bite: If the AI writes my definitions, but it only writes what I need because I've already defined the problem externally to lean, and this is what I prompt it with, and then I am looking over its shoulder and keeping it in line with those definitions, making sure they actually match my theory, did the AI write my definitions? It's blurry, I think.

I'll add: I would wager a fair penny that the AI conforms to Mathlib standards far better than I would be able to. So it's kind of like knowing exactly what needs to be painted at a minimum, but explaining that to a man who can actually paint instead of trying to do it yourself. And then they point out some techniques that will improve your desired painting. That's how I feel about it, at least, after the last few months of intensive work with the AI assisted part of this project.

That said, I am definitely already learning lean and I look forward to not needing AI for much, if at all.

From your description above, yes, this is a primarily AI authored project.

Ian Allen said:

I would wager a fair penny that the AI conforms to Mathlib standards far better than I would be able to.

"better" can be far from "sufficiently" :-)
